title: Cornell's Faculty Senate votes "no confidence" in administration
summary: Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution expressing no confidence in the university's administration, including Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators.
story: Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution expressing no confidence in the university's administration, including Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators.
It's a major rebuke of the university's leadership.
Members of the faculty told CBS News New York the resolution questioned whether Cornell's administration can effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault on campus.
The vote, which passed 75-50, is largely symbolic and does not require university leadership to step down. Five faculty senators abstained and five others did not vote.

"We distanced ourselves from this leadership and said they don't speak for us. They are not the Cornell we know and love," resolution co-sponsor and faculty senator Iris Packman said. "Our vision for Cornell is one of zero tolerance for sexual assault."

The vote follows weeks of outrage over Cornell's handling of sexual assault allegations, including Jane Doe's 2024 alleged gang rape case. All seven men accused of wrongdoing in her lawsuit deny the allegations.
"We created this resolution after hearing from scores of current students, alumni, staff and faculty that the Jane Doe case was the tip of an iceberg," resolution sponsor Paul Ortiz said.

"This vote is a reckoning for our University. It is a call for real, systemic change; not a slow-moving taskforce, weakly enforced ban on fraternity parties, or expensive PR damage control, but meaningful, evidence-based steps to reduce the incidence of sexual assault on campus and provide significant support to and justice for survivors," sponsors of the measure said in a statement.

"We believe that the Faculty Senate did not reach this decision lightly and considered all available information," Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra said in a statement. "We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

"In the 56 years since the establishment of the Faculty Senate at Cornell, the body has never taken such a significant step to condemn the actions of leadership," Cornell's chapter of the American Association of University Professors said in a statement. "President Kotlikoff and [Vice President of Student and Campus Life Ryan] Lombardi have failed in their attention to student well-being and accountability. For Cornell to restore good faith and confidence in democratic governance for shaping positive reforms, there must be a change in leadership."
After the vote, Anne Meinig Smalling, the chair of Cornell's Board of Trustees, said the board "fully supports" Kotlikoff and his administration.

"Today's Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable. There is no place for sexual violence on the Cornell campus. We support President Kotlikoff's commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again," Smalling said. "The Board of Trustees remains confident that President Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus. This confidence is rooted not only in the administration's actions to date and plans moving forward but also in its track record of navigating complex problems, as it did in restoring federal funding, preserving free speech, and leading the University through COVID."

Smalling said Kotlikoff and his administration "have a plan that is focused on strengthening student safety, improving support for survivors, and addressing aspects of our campus culture that must change."
"The Board fully supports President Kotlikoff and his administration as they continue to listen and act decisively in support of students," Smalling said.
She said the independent investigation led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates "will identify what more needs to be fixed."

Kotlikoff has acknowledged shortcomings in the university's response and announced new safety measures, including a ban on fraternity parties and an agreement with New York State Police to investigate sexual assault complaints.
The no-confidence measure's sponsors accused the administration of "repeated attempts to silence us."

"The faculty have come together to express our discontent and to demand that Cornell do better. We are speaking up for our students, colleagues, staff and alumni who have called on us to hold the administration accountable. From addressing the root causes of rape culture on campus to calling out the ways Title IX has been weaponized against survivors, we will use our collective voice to bring about real change," the sponsors said. "We're looking at next steps for concrete change: addressing hazing and fraternity culture; demanding transparency from the administration, including seeing the full Yates report; reforming the Title IX process and sanctions to hold perpetrators accountable; working with outside law enforcement agencies for independent, trauma-informed investigations; and improving support for survivors.
"Now we begin the process of rebuilding our beloved university into what we all know and believe it can be: a place of learning and growth; curiosity and discovery; and safety and belonging."
"This is about the kind of university that we want Cornell to be, and we want it to be one that prioritizes students over reputation," one Cornell student said.

title: DOJ official resigns amid questions about "grand conspiracy" probe
summary: Jason Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, abruptly resigned, marking another high-profile departure from a DOJ inquiry plagued by internal disputes.
story: The top federal prosecutor in South Florida who was overseeing the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation into Obama- and Biden-era intelligence officials abruptly resigned on Friday, marking another high-profile departure from a Justice Department inquiry plagued by internal disputes and doubts about its viability.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the resignation of Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, and praised him for his work tackling violent crime, trafficking and transnational criminal organizations.
The statement offered no explanation for his departure.

In a post on X, Quiñones thanked President Trump for the opportunity and said it had been "the privilege of a lifetime to serve" alongside his colleagues in the Southern District. "I leave with immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great nation," he wrote.

His exit is the latest blow to the investigation based in Fort Pierce, which is probing whether former intelligence officials under two different Democratic administrations conspired to keep Mr. Trump out of office through a series of criminal and intelligence investigations. The probe is also separately focusing on whether former CIA Director John Brennan lied to Congress about the agency's role in the creation of an intelligence assessment that determined Russia had tried to interfere in the 2016 presidential election.

Quiñones' departure comes after Joe diGenova, a former U.S. attorney in Washington, D.C., in the 1980s, also abruptly quit his role in September amid disagreements with the Deputy Attorney General's Office over the management of the investigation.

Things came to a head with diGenova after senior Justice Department leaders sent two attorneys from Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter's office to Florida to try to help manage the case, which both diGenova and Quiñones resisted, sources previously told CBS News.

Since then, Kurt Olsen, a former White House attorney who was known for his efforts to try to overturn the results of the 2020 election, also resigned from the case, while several others who were temporarily assigned to the probe returned to their home U.S. attorney's offices after their details came to an end.

Earlier in the year, the lead career prosecutor in Quiñones' office who was overseeing the investigation was also sidelined after she expressed concerns about the strength of the evidence, CBS News previously reported.

Blanche told reporters in late October that Quiñones "always has been in charge" of the investigation and downplayed prior departures from the investigation, saying "people leave and stay all the time."
"We're going to let that investigation continue as it should," Blanche said, adding, "there's no frustration" with the pace of the probe.
The investigation has generated extensive grand jury activity but has yet to produce charges establishing the alleged overarching conspiracy.

Quiñones' resignation comes just a day after the Justice Department announced the departure of Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division. The son of Cuban refugees, Quiñones has tried to make a name for himself in South Florida by pursuing investigations into communist Cuban government officials who have committed crimes impacting the United States.

Earlier this year, he established a Cuba-focused task force that brought together law enforcement agents from multiple agencies to work on investigations. He also oversaw the criminal prosecution of former Cuban leader Raúl Castro and five others in connection with the Cuban military's fatal downing of two planes 30 years ago.

Separately, his office has also been working on a new criminal investigation targeting former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, who is in a jail in New York City awaiting trial on criminal drug and torture charges, CBS News previously reported.

The Miami-based investigation is focused on corruption, one source previously told CBS News, and began shortly before Alex Saab, a close business associate of Maduro who served as Venezuela's minister of industry and national production, was deported to the U.S. and indicted for his alleged role in a money-laundering conspiracy scheme.
Saab has since pleaded guilty in the case, raising questions among observers about whether he might agree to cooperate and provide prosecutors with evidence against Maduro.

title: Mississippi Senate race still a toss-up; Democrat holds slim lead
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. By Friday afternoon, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.
State officials say several thousand ballots still need to be counted, and both campaigns have expressed confidence.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. The state is also processing an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Mail ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of just two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: Stocks rebound after tech selloff that pushed Nasdaq into correction
summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged up in early trading after a Thursday rout driven by concerns about a potential slowdown in data center construction.
story: Stocks clawed back some of their losses on Friday after a steep selloff the previous day driven by concerns over a potential slowdown in data center construction.

The S&P 500 rose 23 points, or 0.3%, to close at 7,377, failing to erase the sharp losses it suffered Thursday on its worst day since April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended up 1.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.5%.

"Tech is rebounding after two days of some of the most aggressive selling in a long time, although the rally is very tentative and tepid, without much aggressive chasing," Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a note to investors midday Friday.

Financial markets soared immediately after the midterm elections earlier this week, but quickly reversed course on Thursday as investors assessed whether sweeping Democratic victories could lead to tighter restrictions on building data centers and weaker spending on artificial intelligence.

Although Democrats will control both the House and Senate when newly elected lawmakers take office in January, President Trump will retain veto authority, which will likely limit the passage of major restrictions on data centers. Opposition is more likely to surface at the state and local level, Wall Street analysts said.
As of Friday, voters had approved more than 40 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across the country, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting.

Tech stocks started to recover on Friday, helping pull the Nasdaq higher after a brutal beating on Thursday that caused the index to shed more than 1,400 points and enter a "correction," or when stocks fall at least 10% from their previous peak.

Chipmaker Nvidia — a bellwether for the AI sector — gained 2.5% in afternoon trading, and semiconductor manufacturer Micron Technology rose 3.9%. The so-called hyperscalers — the companies leading the data center buildout — saw modest gains, with Google-owner Alphabet climbing 0.8%, Amazon up 0.9% and Meta gaining 2.1%; Microsoft shed 0.6%.

IREN, a company that delivers data centers, compute and software for AI training, reported stronger-than-expected results for its latest quarter. Its stock jumped 19.2%, and it also announced two new contracts signed since the end of the quarter.
"We own the land, the power and the data centers under all of it, which gives us more ways to fund growth and lets us set its pace," co-CEO Daniel Roberts said.
Outside of AI, markets were mixed, and more S&P 500 stocks fell than rose.
Slowing AI investment?

A key question for Wall Street is whether AI companies will deliver the revenue growth investors are banking on. Anthropic, which filed for an initial public offering last month and is expected to debut on the Nasdaq this month, will serve as a critical test case. While filing highlighted rapid growth, the company has yet to turn a profit.

In a research note on Friday, Vicky Redwood, a chief economic adviser at Capital Economics, said the investment advisory firm expects AI to boost productivity but is "less confident that AI revenues will grow rapidly enough to sustain the current pace of investment."
The firm expects AI capital expenditures to slow next year, a development Redwood said could drag on U.S. economic growth.

The stock market rebound on Friday came after the release of the jobs report, which showed robust payroll gains in October. Employers added 165,000 last month, above economists' expectations, while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%.
The burst in hiring increases the odds that Federal Reserve officials will raise interest rates at their next meeting in December and in 2027, according to Wall Street economists.

"A solid October jobs report leaves the Fed free to focus on inflation. We expect rate increases in December and March, with energy and AI spillovers the main risks to inflation," Oxford Economics said in a report.

title: Rob Sand's runway modeling past resurfaces after Iowa gubernatorial win
summary: Vogue asked on Instagram whether followers knew the Iowa governor-elect once modeled for Prada. A verified account for Sand, who was previously elected to the Iowa state auditor's office, replied affirmatively in the comments.
story: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who won Tuesday's election, walked runways for Prada and other fashion houses while he was in college, according to Vogue.

Vogue asked on Instagram whether followers knew that Sand once modeled for Prada. A verified account for Sand, @robsandia, replied in the comments Thursday: "Yes, I knew that." The comment had more than 700 likes about 20 minutes later, and many replies were congratulatory.
"From runway to run USA ✨," one comment read, while another enthused, "THE biggest flex EVER for a politician plus 2 words: Italian Vogue. YES SIR! 👏 🔥"

Vogue reported that the modeling past surfaced on social media after his win, when a user reposted a video of Sand with a caption expressing disbelief that he once modeled. A Google search confirmed it, Vogue said.

The New York Times earlier reported, in a 2019 profile, that Sand briefly modeled in Paris and Milan while in college but does not like to talk about it. However, Sand's campaign confirmed to CBS News that he "did some modeling while in college in the early 2000s." And on X, formerly known as Twitter, Sand's campaign joked, "Audited: true." (Sand was previously elected to serve as Iowa's state auditor.)

Sand began modeling while attending Brown University, which Vogue described as a successful side hustle that took him to Milan. He walked for Prada, the Japanese label Number (N)ine and Giuliano Fujiwara, and appeared in editorial spreads, including a fall 2002 AnOther Magazine spread titled "Adolescents," Vogue reported.
Sand also previously told Newsweek that he missed a chance to caucus in 2004 in his hometown of Decorah, Iowa, because he was in Milan.
Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn in Tuesday's race for governor earlier this week.

title: Newly empowered Democrats could revive plans for court reforms
summary: Democrats have proposed a variety of measures aimed at reshaping the Supreme Court over the years and may be poised to push them forward after winning House and Senate majorities.
story: Washington — After years of calling for reforms to the Supreme Court following blockbuster decisions on abortion, presidential power and voting rights, Democrats may be poised to push forward with their court-focused plans after winning control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Democrats are expected to hold at least 54 seats in the Senate and at least 250 members in the House, giving them the opportunity to take up legislation that stood no chance of advancing in the GOP-led Congress.

While Democrats have not yet unveiled their legislative priorities for the next Congress, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be elected speaker in January, has indicated he has the Supreme Court on his mind.

"We must root out corrupt price gouging, clean up the mess at the Supreme Court and ban Members of Congress from trading stocks," he wrote in a letter to his Democratic colleagues formally announcing his bid for the speaker's gavel. "Accountability begins at home."

Jeffries told NBC's "Meet the Press" in August that "dramatic" reform to the Supreme Court is needed, and said Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who will likely helm the House Judiciary Committee in the next Congress, would take the lead. A spokesperson for Raskin did not immediately return a request for comment.
Over the years, Democrats have proposed a variety of measures aimed at reshaping the Supreme Court — from implementing term limits for the justices to laying out new ethics rules to adding seats.

During the first two years of the Biden administration, when Democrats last controlled Congress, the House approved legislation that would have imposed ethics requirements on Supreme Court justices. But the measure stalled in the Senate.

Then-President Joe Biden established a commission tasked with studying proposals to reform the high court, but the panel did not recommend structural changes and instead laid out the arguments in support of and against potential changes.

But calls for Supreme Court reforms have grown louder since Democrats were last in charge, particularly as the court's conservative majority has overturned longstanding precedents and expanded executive authority.

With Democrats now holding a majority in the House, members could push through legislation imposing changes on the high court. Still, it's unlikely those plans would clear the Senate, where most legislation requires 60 votes to advance. Democrats will control between 54 and 56 seats. And even if court-reform measures did win approval from both chambers of Congress, it's unclear whether Mr. Trump would sign them into law.
Here are some of the proposals that Democrats could take up in the next Congress:
Ethics reforms

Legislative efforts aimed at requiring the Supreme Court to adopt a code of conduct gained momentum in 2023, after ProPublica published a series of articles about Justice Clarence Thomas's trips with a wealthy Republican donor that were omitted from his financial disclosures.

On the heels of the revelations, the Senate Judiciary Committee advanced legislation that would require the Supreme Court to adopt an ethics code and implement procedures to handle complaints of misconduct. But the proposal from Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, died before the full Senate.
Whitehouse reintroduced the proposal in May 2025. Rep. Hank Johnson, a Georgia Democrat, introduced companion legislation in the House.

Whitehouse and Johnson's legislation would also require the Supreme Court to establish rules for the disclosure of gifts, income or reimbursements, including a requirement that parties to a case or people filing friend-of-the-court briefs must disclose any gifts to the justices.

Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Rep. Daniel Goldman of New York also introduced plans that would require the Supreme Court to establish an internal Office of Ethics Counsel and Office of Investigative Counsel. The investigative counsel would review and investigate ethics complaints against the justices.
A measure from Maryland's Raskin and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York would prohibit federal judges and Supreme Court justices from receiving gifts valued at more than $50.
The Supreme Court did put its own code of conduct in place in November 2023, but its lack of an enforcement mechanism led to calls for Congress to step in.

Beyond the Supreme Court, a Democratic-led Congress could also investigate claims of misconduct by federal judges on the lower courts that have recently become public, said Gabe Roth, executive director of Fix the Court, which advocates for reforms to the Supreme Court and lower courts.
Some federal judges have been accused of mistreating their clerks. Others have been investigated for alleged misconduct.

U.S. District Judge Eleanor Ross in Georgia received a private reprimand after an investigation found she had sex with a police officer in her chambers. GOP Rep. Andrew Clyde of Georgia has filed articles of impeachment against her.

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown in Texas is facing judicial conduct proceedings after she was accused of making racial insults toward a lawyer, judges and court staff, and recusing from dozens of cases without explanation or for "unusual" reasons.
"There's 2,400 federal judges, so there's going to be a few bad apples, but if we're going to talk about cleaning up the government, we can't leave out the third branch," Roth said.

Congressional Democrats could also enact legislation expanding workplace discrimination and harassment laws to cover the judiciary, an idea that has gotten bipartisan support before, and ban Supreme Court justices and judges from trading stocks and using prediction markets, Roth said.

"The larger issue is really in the lower courts and resetting the rules of the road and making it clear that while there may have been a focus on the Supreme Court over the last three years, the lower courts really shouldn't be immune from this anticorruption push," he said.
Term limits
Article III of the Constitution states that Supreme Court justices and lower court judges hold their seats "during good behavior," which has been interpreted to mean that judges have life tenure.
But Democrats in Congress have argued that justices should be subject to term limits and rolled out proposals establishing those rules through legislation and constitutional amendments.
Several bills introduced in the House would set 18-year term limits for justices and establish regular appointments in certain years of a president's term.

Under one of the proposals for a constitutional amendment, introduced by Maryland Democratic Rep. Johnny Olszewski, sitting justices who have been on the court for more than 18 years would have to retire. Chief Justice John Roberts, Justice Samuel Alito and Thomas have all served more than 18 years.

One of the term-limit plans comes from a Republican lawmaker, Rep. Tom Barrett of Michigan. His proposal for a constitutional amendment would limit terms for members of the Supreme Court and lower courts to 20 years.
Barrett lost his seat for reelection in Tuesday's midterms.

Amending the Constitution requires Congress to pass a joint resolution with support from two-thirds of both the House and Senate. Then, the proposal must be ratified by three-fourths of the states, or 38 or 50 states.
Expanding the Supreme Court

The Constitution does not set the number of justices on the Supreme Court, and across the nation's history, the number of people on the high court has changed six times, ranging from a low of six justices to a high of 10. There have been nine justices since 1869.
But there's been a groundswell of calls from some Democrats for Supreme Court expansion, particularly in the wake of contentious decisions on abortion, regulatory authority  and presidential power.

One bill, from Democratic Rep. Al Green of Texas, was introduced this year and would grow the number of seats on the Supreme Court from nine to 13. Past proposals from Democrats in the House and Senate would also add four seats to the high court.

title: Stocks crater as midterms spur investor exodus from tech and AI
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq is now in a "correction" as Wall Street weighs the impact of the Democrats' wins on the critical AI sector.
story: The stock market tanked on Thursday amid concerns that a shift in congressional political control following the U.S. midterm elections could slow the construction of data centers that power artificial intelligence services.

Stocks sank across the board, but technology companies with a hand in the AI sector were hit especially hard. The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 1,422 points, or 5.5%, to close at 24,315. The drop means the tech-heavy index is now in a "correction," or down more than 10% from its most recent all-time high, set in October.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 335 points, or 4.4%, to end at 7,354, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,833 points, or 3.4%.

The decline continued on markets in Europe and Asia on Friday but U.S. shares were set to trade mixed. Dow futures were down 0.8% at 51,192.00. S&P 500 futures gained ground, adding almost 0.3% to 7,402.50.

Market watchers think the Democrats' sweeping electoral victories this week could bolster opponents of data centers and slow the rollout of the facilities, which have spurred widespread public opposition. Investors are reacting to the growing "headline" risks around AI, according to Wall Street analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge.

The rout was violent enough to potentially delay the highly anticipated initial public offering by Anthropic, a bellwether for the entire AI business, Crisafulli told investors in a research note. Before the turmoil in financial markets, the IPO had been expected to take place this month and to raise as much as $100 billion.

The sharp drop also marks a sharp reversal from Wednesday, when the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year. Other indexes also surged after the election results eased uncertainty about who will control Washington.
"Visible cracks"

"Even though the market rallied Wednesday after the midterm elections, there were visible cracks in the AI ecosystem, and they widened on Thursday amid investor concerns about a potentially slower data center buildout with Democrats in charge of Congress," Chris Larkin, a managing director of trading and investing for E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, said in an email.
A slowdown in erecting data centers could deal a major blow to AI companies, which are pouring billions into the buildout and banking on widespread adoption of the technology.

"The trigger for these moves appears to be the concern that the Democrats, both in Congress and at the state level, will seek to regulate the AI industry and restrict data center development," Joe Maher, markets economist with investment adviser Capital Economics, said in a report. "The immediate risk is that restrictions on data center construction slow the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout. That is an obvious headwind for the firms directly involved in that buildout, whose prospects depend on continued rapid capex growth.
Investors worry that the enormous investment in AI is creating a stock market bubble, which happens when sky-high valuations become detached from companies' underlying fundamentals.
"Whether the midterms shock turns out to be the catalyst that derails the AI equity boom remains to be seen, but it strengthens our sense that the boom is in its final innings," Maher said.

Chip and other AI-exposed stocks took a particular beating on Thursday. Shares of Nvidia, whose advanced chips are a key component in developing ever more powerful AI models, fell 9.2% a day after dropping 3.2%. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8%.

Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform, also continued to flail, with its shares falling 10.5% after dropping nearly 25% on Wednesday. The stock, which now hovers around $4, is at an all-time low since the company publicly listed its shares in March of 2024.

In other financial markets, the initial reaction to the election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6% to $97.11 and recovered much of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.

title: Feds warn of potential cyberattacks on industrial refrigerators
summary: After a wave of attacks in Europe, U.S. officials are warning of "ongoing" cyber threats targeting refrigeration systems used in healthcare, agriculture and other industries.
story: The U.S. government encouraged grocery stores, healthcare facilities and other businesses that use commercial refrigeration to tighten their security measures on Thursday following a series of cyberattacks that remotely changed the temperatures of commercial freezers and fridges across Europe.

Five federal agencies issued a joint notice, warning of "ongoing cyber threat activity" that could target refrigeration systems used across healthcare, agriculture, transportation and other U.S. industries.
Bad actors globally are exploiting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in refrigeration systems that are "unpatched" or connected to the internet, the agencies said.

"If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system," the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said in a statement, which was issued in conjunction with the FBI, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Agriculture and Department of Transportation.

In a fact sheet, CISA said businesses that rely on industrial refrigeration should take precautions to protect their systems, including changing passwords, disconnecting system devices from the internet and making software updates to address vulnerabilities.

"Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,"  Chris Butera, acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity at CISA, said in a statement.
The agencies did not specify if any refrigeration systems have been targeted in the U.S.
Wave of refrigeration attacks

The warning follows reports of refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases in August. The Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, a U.S. federal law enforcement unit, has launched an investigation into the incidents, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News on Thursday.

Similar incidents have occurred around Europe in recent weeks, with hackers targeting fridges and freezers across numerous grocery chains. Food retailers reported unexpected temperature spikes in their refrigeration systems, causing food to spoil in stores in Luxembourg, Belgium and Sweden.

Officials in France, which has also been hit by grocery store cyberattacks, said on Wednesday that its national emergency blood supply network was targeted by hackers who tried to raise refrigeration temperatures at several blood banks.

Joshua Corman, executive-in-residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology, a security think tank, said he expects more such attacks, warning that refrigeration systems used by medical labs, grocery stores and bulk warehouses in the U.S. could be compromised.
"There's only so many players that do industrial-level refrigeration, and they're likely also just as vulnerable," he told CBS News.

title: Trump library plans on collision course with Democratic Congress
summary: President Trump is expected to spend time on plans for his presidential library, but Democrats in Congress have some questions about how it's being financed.
story: As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."
With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.
"The donors bankrolling his personal vanity project will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told CBS News.

In March, Mr. Trump shared renderings of a 47-story tower on a donated plot in downtown Miami. It showed golden escalators, a full-size Air Force One and a giant statue of him raising his fist, as he did after surviving an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. But then he told reporters he does not "believe in building libraries or museums" and that the building is "most likely going to be a hotel," a departure from the traditional library his foundation described to the IRS last year.

The Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit, registered in Florida and run by Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, will fund the project. The foundation says it expects to raise $950 million by the end of 2027, including $600 million in 2027 alone, according to its October 2025 IRS application, obtained by CBS News. That far outpaces what Mr. Trump's predecessors had raised at this stage.

Tens of millions of dollars have already come from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. The nonprofit is also collecting donations through a payment processing company that has Donald Trump Jr. on its board, according to a fundraising portal page. And Mr. Trump has said the luxury Boeing 747 that Qatar gave the U.S. last year — now in use as Air Force One — would go to the library, though Eric Trump and the White House have since said that plan is not final.

Some of the most recent money has come from people trying to stay in Mr. Trump's good graces. After the president threatened to cut ties with his top political advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair over their consulting work for a pro-Russian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the two men donated their fees from that work to the library, The New York Post reported.

A week later, The New York Times reported that Mr. Trump had told aides and allies that his former personal lawyer, Alina Habba Mildon, should donate part of a contract worth more than $50 million to his library or another Trump-related entity. Habba Mildon's contract was with a company tied to the family of a Venezuelan businessman Mr. Trump pardoned in January, the outlet reported.

Asked by CBS News whether she planned to donate some of her fees to the library, Habba Mildon responded to the text message with a "haha" reaction. (She removed the reaction seconds later and declined to comment.)

A former Trump adviser, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the library is now where the fundraising action is, with the midterms over and donors already tapped for the America 250 celebrations and the White House ballroom. MAGA Inc., a super PAC run by Mr. Trump's allies, started September with more than $400 million to spend on Republicans in the midterms. Its filing due in December will show how much left it has in cash on hand.
"The library is one of the last few places he can squeeze people for money," the former adviser said. "That's what a businessman does. He just creates opportunities."

Fresh scrutiny of the library is expected after Democrats swept the House and the Senate on Tuesday. Starting in January, Democrats will have the power to subpoena records and compel testimony. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word warning on X to the administration after the election results: "Lawyer up."

"Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," Warren told CBS News, adding that she will be investigating the library "and any wrongdoing will be held accountable."

The library has already drawn scrutiny over Mr. Trump's stated plan to display the gifted jet. The plane's memorandum of understanding, signed in 2025 by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Qatar's Minister of State for Defense Affairs Soud bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, called it an "unconditional donation." But when questions were raised about the U.S. accepting and using the Qatari plane as Air Force One, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi concluded that the gift could be conditioned on transferring the plane to the library foundation by Jan. 1, 2029, about three weeks before Mr. Trump leaves office.
In August, Eric Trump told NBC News that displaying the plane was "not the plan at the moment," saying a retired Air Force One would be shown instead.

A Qatari official, speaking to CBS News on the condition of anonymity, said what happens to the plane after Mr. Trump leaves office is not Qatar's concern. "This is something the Americans need to deal with," the official said.
The White House referred questions about the library and whether any final decisions have been made about the plane or a hotel to the foundation, which did not respond to requests for comment.

"The Trump Presidential Library will be one of the most magnificent buildings in the world and a living testament to the indelible impact President Trump has made on America and its people," Davis Ingle, a spokesman for the White House, said in a statement.
Tens of millions from companies Mr. Trump sued

There have been two iterations of the library's nonprofit funding structure. The first, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Fund, was incorporated in Florida in December 2024, days after ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward the library to settle a defamation suit over anchor George Stephanopoulos' inaccurate on-air claim that Mr. Trump had been found civilly liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found him liable for sexual abuse.

Other settlements followed. Meta agreed to pay $22 million toward the library over the suspension of Mr. Trump's accounts after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Elon Musk's X paid $10 million to settle a similar suit by Mr. Trump and other plaintiffs. And Paramount paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.

By then, the current foundation had been incorporated in Florida in May 2025, listing Eric Trump, Boulos and James Kiley, an attorney who has represented Mr. Trump, as trustees. The original fund was dissolved that September after failing to file a required annual report. Jacob Roth, an attorney who incorporated the first fund, declined to comment.

In March, Sens. Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Melanie Stansbury asked the four companies for details of their payments. ABC said its $15 million was still in an escrow account held by a law firm representing Mr. Trump, where it had been since December 2024, awaiting release to the foundation. Paramount said it had paid $16 million but did not say to whom. Meta said $22 million had been "designated" for the library but did not say whether or where it was paid, and X, citing confidentiality, did not say how much of its $10 million settlement went there.

Mr. Trump's financial disclosure, filed in June, lists $56.5 million in settlement money from ABC, Meta and Paramount as paid to the foundation. It lists $8 million from X as paid to Mr. Trump himself, without saying whether some funds reached the foundation. The foundation's October 2025 filing with Florida charity regulators, which it labeled a proposed budget, projected $50 million in revenue and about $6 million in spending.

Meta and ABC declined to comment. X did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Skydance referred CBS News to the company's July 2025 statement announcing the settlement, which said the $16 million included the plaintiffs' legal fees and costs and that the remainder would go to Mr. Trump's future presidential library, with nothing paid to him personally.

The settlements are not the only large gifts. SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant, told Congress in July that it gave the foundation $50 million in January to support a library exhibit highlighting U.S.-Japan relations. Two months later, Mr. Trump's Energy Department announced it would lease federal land at a former uranium enrichment plant in Ohio to an affiliate of SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for a data center campus that the company says will be the world's largest for artificial intelligence.

A spokesperson for the Energy Department said the agency signed its lease agreement with the company on Feb. 26, about a month after SoftBank's donation to the library foundation. They added that a local development group first proposed the project in October 2024, before SoftBank acquired the lease rights in the fall of 2025. SoftBank did not respond to a request for comment.
A library or a hotel?

The library foundation's filings offer few other details about how it operates. When it registered as a charity in Florida, the foundation said its officers did not expect to be paid. But in its application to the IRS, the foundation said it would pay its leaders. It projected spending $400,000 on compensation in 2025, rising to $1.2 million in 2027. The foundation's bylaws say trustees can't be paid, but other roles can come with compensation. Eric Trump is both a trustee and the foundation's president.
The foundation told CBS News it expects to file financial disclosures covering fiscal 2025 by Nov. 15. It did not respond to a question about whether Eric Trump will be paid.
Fundraising for the library is led by Meredith O'Rourke, who has worked with Mr. Trump since 2016.

The foundation also raises money through PSQ Impact, a donation platform run by PublicSquare, a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr. The foundation's donation page says contributions will "help preserve important archives, promote civic education, and inspire generations to come." Trump Jr. began receiving $42,000 a month in consulting fees from PublicSquare in August 2024, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he was not aware of the fundraising page and had no involvement in it. PublicSquare did not respond to questions about how much has been raised through the donation page or what fee, if any, it is charging for processing.

"This is just one example of many where the Trumps are set to possibly profit off something connected to Donald Trump's presidency," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen.

It remains unclear what form the library will ultimately take. Mr. Trump's suggestion that it could become a hotel is cited in a lawsuit filed in May by Miami residents, a local nonprofit and a Miami Dade College student. They argue that Florida's gift of the 2.63-acre parcel, a former college parking lot, violates a U.S. constitutional provision that bars states from giving the president financial benefits.

The land was appraised at more than $67 million, but the suit cites real estate experts who say its true market value is over $300 million. The plaintiffs note that the state's terms require only that the site include "components of a Presidential library, museum, and/or center" within five years, and do not preclude a hotel.

Other presidential libraries have been built on donated public land. Chicago leased parkland for Mr. Obama's center for $10, and Little Rock used eminent domain to assemble the site for Mr. Clinton's. But Florida conveyed its parcel outright.

The Justice Department has argued that Mr. Trump is immune from the suit. In September, U.S. District Judge Rodolfo Ruiz II, a Trump appointee, halted discovery, writing that the defendants' arguments for dismissal, including presidential immunity, "may prove to be successful." He has not yet ruled on motions to dismiss the case, and a ruling may not come until March, according to Gerald E. Greenberg, a lawyer for the plaintiffs.
If the suit is dismissed, Greenberg said the plaintiffs are likely to appeal.

"This case is really about one of the core anti-corruption provisions," Greenberg told CBS News, saying the founders "understood the dangers of people currying favor with the sovereign by giving him gifts."
"It is extremely disturbing to think of our skyline and our downtown being blighted by this monument to corruption," he added.

title: Mass shooting in Polish market leaves at least 6 dead, 15 injured
summary: Krakow police said a man who had driven onto the square began firing at random people from his car.
story: A man drove into an open market in the Polish city of Krakow and opened fire from his car, killing at least six people and injuring at least 15 others, authorities said. The shooter was shot by police and taken into custody.

The shooting happened in the Main Market Square in Krakow around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday. Krakow police said the alleged shooter began firing at random people from his car. Police said the victims were four women and two men.
Marcin Kierwiński, Poland's interior minister, said there were indications the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideology, according to Reuters.

Police officers are among the wounded. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a confrontation with police a short distance away from the initial violence, and was taken to a hospital for treatment.
The death toll earlier stood at five, but the Malopolski regional government updated it to six in a post on X.
Kierwiński wrote on X that two police officers were wounded by gunfire and one is in serious condition.
"Police officers in Kraków risked their lives to intervene. Immediately. Thanks to their heroic actions, the attacker was quickly apprehended," he wrote.
In a social media post, Krakow police said the gunman is a Polish citizen and that he acted alone.

Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the suspected gunman was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many pieces of other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car.

"I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow following the tragic shooting," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on social media, adding that "the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack."
He later headed to Krakow from the capital, Warsaw, a government spokesperson said.
Other details were not immediately available.
Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.
"The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted to X.

"We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that's shattered the peace of Poland," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X. "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow."
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, a European Union and NATO member of 38 million people.

"I saw a man shooting at people and walking around the square," Annette, a woman in her sixties, told news wire Agence France-Presse. "It's a tragedy for Krakow; we've never seen anything like this before."
Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said in a statement that the EU stands with Poland and offered her condolences.

"The tragic loss of life in the shooting in Kraków is a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland," she wrote on X. "Poland's strength lies in the resilience of its people. In this moment of grief, Poland does not stand alone."
Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 155 miles from the capital, Warsaw.

title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government
summary: Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but neither won a clear majority.
story: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leading a bloc of parties seeking to oust Israel's longest-serving premier.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu's party won a clear majority in the vote. But in marathon discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government.
Herzog's decision is a setback for Netanyahu, who has alleged election interference by Arab countries.

The acting director-general of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."
This is a developing news story and will be updated.

title: Pope Leo calls for universal healthcare weeks after lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV spoke about access to healthcare on his first stop in Uruguay during his 12-day Latin American tour.
story: Montevideo - Pope Leo XIV drew on his own recent experience of illness and hospitalization after surgery for lung cancer on Friday to make an impassioned appeal for universal access to healthcare, greater social equality and a society that does not measure people's worth by their productivity or wealth.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness and I received care for which I am grateful," the Pope said in his first speech after arriving in Uruguay, to the country's political and civic leaders.

Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital four days after removing a cancerous tumor from his right lung.  "The experience made me think of the many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis or receive the treatment they need."
"Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society," he said.

Uruguay is the first stop of a 12-day trip that also includes Argentina and Peru. Leo's doctors said he needed no further treatment after his operation and was cleared to travel. The trip schedule is the longest international journey of his pontificate so far, with 19,000 travel miles, 14 flights, 36 speeches and approximately 50 events.

Vatican officials told reporters ahead of the trip that the Pope would have a medical team travel with him, as is customary on papal trips, but that no special measures were being taken. "We're speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health," the Vatican spokesman said.

The Latin America journey is Leo's first return as Pope to the country and region that has profoundly shaped his vision, and where he spent decades of his life, first as an Augustinian missionary, and then as bishop of Chiclayo, Peru. The pope holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
Leo's remarks on caring for the sick were part of a broad appeal for a society where the most vulnerable are protected, and where economic development benefits everyone rather than just the elite.
"The creation of wealth and economic initiative…must also translate into goods and opportunities that effectively reach everyone," Leo said.

While praising Uruguay for four decades of uninterrupted democracy, he stressed that a country's success is ultimately measured by how it protects human dignity and cares for the most vulnerable in society.
Leo also spoke in defense of children, including the unborn. Abortion was legalized in Uruguay in 2012, making it one of the first Latin American countries to do so.
"Their absolute dependence on their mother does not diminish the dignity to which they are entitled or the protection they deserve," the pope said.

Children, he said, must have access to quality education and opportunities to enter the workforce and achieve personal independence.  Touching on a subject close to his heart, he said that technological advances and artificial intelligence must serve human beings rather than replace workers.

Leo will remain in Uruguay until Sunday when he will continue his travels to Argentina and Peru. The Vatican spokesman said there, Leo would address a range of issues, including the environment, arms tracking and political instability.
The Pope will also hold meetings with survivors of clerical sex abuse, but no further details are available as of now.

title: Zelenskyy says Russia is stepping up attacks ahead of U.S. talks
summary: Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi for talks aimed at ending the war.
story: Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media that Russia used 36 missiles to target critical infrastructure. Only four missiles were taken down, Zelenskyy said, highlighting a shortage of interceptors. He also said 172 drones were used in the attacks, which struck Kyiv and 12 other regions.
The president accused Russia of intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and the country's infrastructure ahead of trilateral talks.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
"Russia has a very particular view of diplomacy – as a subtype of aggression," Zelenskyy wrote.
"We hope that the United States, like our other partners, will act on principle," he added.
Russian attacks target Ukrainian infrastructure
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
Zelenskyy said a kindergarten was "partially destroyed." Photos show rubble near the damaged building.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.

"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"

Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 892-yard-long Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River. Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."

Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.

Russia also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.

Zelenskyy said that at one energy facility, preliminary findings show Russia used KN-23 missiles "manufactured and supplied by North Korea." He called the use of the alleged North Korean missile "further proof that global sanctions regimes need to be significantly strengthened." Technical assessments at other sites are ongoing.
Recovery efforts continue after massive attack

Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.

"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Russia reports drone strikes
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.

The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

title: Paraguay's president under house arrested after bank collapse
summary: The president was placed under house arrest after being removed from office following the collapse of a bank linked to the government.
story: Paraguay's president has been placed on house arrest on Friday after the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country's population out of their accounts.

Paraguay's Senate voted to remove Santiago Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship in 1989.
Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country's worst political crisis in more than a decade.

Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asunción until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.
The Paraguayan president denied wrongdoing.

When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can't reach their money.

The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says $21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay's bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guaraní has slid against the dollar.

Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97% of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

title: Pope voted in U.S. election because he's "proud to be an American"
summary: Pope Leo, who is on a 12-day, three-country trip in Latin America, also said he credits God and doctors for his lung cancer surgery recovery.
story: Pope Leo XIV, who became the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election, said Friday he is "proud to be an American and to exercise my right" to vote.

His remarks, made to reporters en route to Latin America for a 12-day trip, come after the Vatican confirmed the U.S.-born pontiff had voted via mail-in ballot in his native Chicago. He declined to comment on the outcome of the midterm elections, which gave control of Congress to the Democrats in a repudiation of President Trump. Instead, he pointed to the statement released by the Vatican last week that cited his longstanding belief in civic participation.
The pope, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said in an Oct. 30 statement.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican said in a statement.

The pope has a long history of civic engagement in the U.S., the Vatican said, confirming that during his nearly two decades as a missionary and then bishop in Peru, Leo voted whenever he was eligible. He holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.
The Associated Press reported Leo, as Robert Prevost, previously voted in five primary elections since 2000 — on the Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2019 and Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
Leo said Friday that he hadn't been able to vote in Peru's recent election since absentee ballots "aren't possible."
"But I would have done it. It's a good thing," he said, according to the AP.
U.S. federal law allows American citizens, even those who work for foreign governments, to retain their citizenship.

The 71-year-old pope is on a three-nation, 12-day tour just three weeks after he underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. He was cleared to travel on Oct. 26 — two weeks after his surgery.

"I am very happy to be here myself. I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place," Leo told reporters when he greeted them in the back of the plane. "I confess that from the first day, I had no doubt. I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape."
He acknowledged, though, that he hadn't had a chance to play tennis yet.
"Not yet, but I will," he said.

On Oct. 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of Leo's right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.

"Early detection is obviously the best way to go, and so regular checkups are a blessing," Leo said, crediting his recovery to "trusting God, good doctors, good surgeons, and overall I think a healthy lifestyle."

title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
summary: It was reported in October that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday in Florida in connection with allegations he possessed child sex abuse material in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.
The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.

The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

Markle, who made his first court appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday, entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing black pants and a black T-shirt with an illustration of a cat drinking a tropical drink.

Markle was advised that this hearing was related to the items found in two storage units in California. Prosecutors said they have not made a determination on whether he stays in Florida or is transferred to California, where the charges originated.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas Wilson ordered Markle released on personal recognizance and ordered him to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.
No plea was taken. Markle's arraignment date in the Central District of California is not yet scheduled, but likely won't happen for at least several weeks.
The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.
Allegations in Philippines lead to U.S. and Mexican investigations

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."
The Daily Mail reported last week that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.
In a statement on Friday, the Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."
DOJ's claims against Markle Sr.

According to an affidavit in the complaint filed in federal court, the investigation in the Philippines led law enforcement to investigate two storage units registered to Markle Sr. in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008, with the most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Inside the units, agents with the FBI seized 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse materials. In one of the units, agents found at least 18 images that appear to constitute child pornography.
Two of the images found allegedly show an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle Sr. — with a nude prepubescent girl, the affidavit said.

A third image allegedly shows a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photos allegedly show Markle Sr. with children in various stages of undress, the affidavit said.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement, adding: "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide."
If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
Meghan distanced herself because of allegations years ago

After the reports of the investigation were made public, Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News that she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Meghan also confronted her father last year about the child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, according to CBS News partner BBC News. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025.
According to the BBC, in that letter, Meghan wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet her and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.
Meghan will not be commenting on the arrest at this time, sources say.
