title: Ukrainian official sees hope for eventual Putin-Zelenskyy meeting
summary: Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February.
story: KYIV, Ukraine — Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, expressed "restrained optimism" there could be progress made toward an eventual meeting between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin during trilateral negotiations next week.

Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February and the first since a heated back-and-forth over SpaceX's Starshield being throttled down. In an interview with CBS News on Friday, Budanov said the discussions would focus on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia.

"There are absolutely different situations at different times," Budanov said, referring to these trilateral discussions versus the ones in February. "Now, obviously, all parties wanted to hold this meeting. This means that there are certain prerequisites for this."
"These negotiations are not the last," he said.

Budanov, who led the country's Defense Intelligence service before taking over Ukraine's Presidential Office in January, will join the delegation led by Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to represent Washington. Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Vladimir Putin aide who headed Moscow's team in earlier rounds of negotiations.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said in announcing the talks earlier this week.

The meeting follows several weeks of strain in the U.S.-Ukraine relationship. In October, President Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to supply diesel to the United States for the first time since 2022. Elon Musk's SpaceX also imposed limits on Ukraine's Starshield satellite networks, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and some air-defense systems, before reinstating access weeks later.
Despite these developments, Budanov said he is optimistic about Ukraine's relationship with the United States heading into the trilateral meeting next week.

"Look, it's bad. It shouldn't be like that," Budanov said of the Starshield failures. "But along with that, we can remind you that this situation is resolved in one way or another. This gives optimism for the future."

The trilateral meeting comes as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Strikes this week hit energy facilities in 10 regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry, left hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and cut water to much of Kyiv for more than 16 hours.
Budanov, speaking from his office in the capital, said Russia was using the strikes to create political pressure on Kyiv.

Russia's goal is "to cause the maximum damage to our critical infrastructure," he said. "What they hope to do is to create a foundation for social dissatisfaction, for street protests, and to stifle the national interests. But this will not happen."

title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
summary: At least 20 flights in Europe deal with bomb threats, adding to what one expert calls an unusual level of hoaxes in a short time period, suggesting "a very deliberate act."
story: Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."

British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.
At least two more European flights, along with several Irish and British news outlets, got similar threats on Friday.

No authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats, but Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare."

David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats to commercial flights this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption."

"The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."

Kaminski-Morrow noted that, under an international aviation convention in place for more than 80 years, the pilot in command of a flight has the final authority over its safety, "and airlines always take threats to safety seriously. The business consequences alone of not doing so, even if the threat is proven to be a hoax, would be prohibitive – and you can imagine the cost if it turned out to be genuine."
The flights impacted on Thursday included:

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

The threats to commercial airliners Thursday came after at least seven other flights across Europe received bomb threats this week that prompted aircraft searches, diversions and in at least one other case an escort by an Italian fighter jet.
Some of the threats have been sent to airlines by email, but the nature of all of the messages has not been confirmed.
Hoaxes, but on an unusual scale

The British government described the incidents in a statement on Tuesday as hoaxes and stressed that the U.K. had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today," according to CBS News' partner network BBC.
Air transport security expert Paul Mason told BBC that threats to passenger planes "don't happen that frequently," making this week's spate of incidents "unusual."

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told the BBC's Radio 5 Live show. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
"There are a lot of processes" that airline crew members and ground staff go through "to validate the credibility of the threat," he said.

While no individual or group has claimed responsibility for any of this week's threats, and no government or security official has pointed the finger at any, the incidents come amid rising concern in Europe about state actors, chiefly Russia and Iran, orchestrating low-level sabotage operations to undermine security on the continent.
The growing "hybrid warfare" battlefield

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by the government, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."
"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said.

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad as the Polish prime minister said suspicious activity was seen on the Russian side, and that the fast security response may have prevented a "serious provocation."

The flight threats also come amid a wave of cyberattacks targeting European grocery store chains' refrigerators and freezers, and even French blood banks. The hacks have forced thousands of pounds of food to be discarded in several countries, but French authorities said security systems prevented the loss of any blood stored in cooling units.
Nobody has claimed responsibility for, or been blamed for the hacks on commercial refrigeration units as of Thursday.
Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.
MI6 boss McCallum, in his remarks last month, said Iran in particular was "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.

McCallum noted in particular "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

Barry Andrews, an Irish Member of the European Parliament, referred to the diverted Aer Lingus flight to Rome on Thursday in a social media post, saying: "This after several hybrid threats and attacks across Europe, and ahead of the major European summit in #Dublin next week. Does anyone still deny Ireland faces serious security threats?"

title: Doomsday cult leader learns fate for murders of 190 children
summary: Paul Mackenzie was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.
story: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people.

The High Court in Kenya's coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.

Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the "primary criminal culpability" for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death.

Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency.
On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of the accused guilty of the murder of 191 people.

In 2023, more than 400 bodies were exhumed from shallow graves on the 800-acre Chakama Ranch in coastal Kilifi County, where Mackenzie's followers lived in mud huts, away from the scrutiny of local communities and authorities.
More than 60 bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, while many others remain unidentified and unclaimed.
During the sentencing, Kavedza said that 183 victims died of starvation, defined as a complete lack of food, and the other eight were classified as murder by direct homicide.

Kavedza said the killings were "cold and calculated" and dismissed claims by some of the accused that the loss of their own children altered the fact that they had participated in the killings of many other children.

The justice said that the perpetrators didn't show remorse and declared they were ready to fast to death as well. During the sentencing, Mackenzie often smiled and chatted with his assistant pastor, Smart Mwakalama, who was sentenced to 160 years in prison.
The prosecution had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie and life imprisonment for his accomplices.
Mackenzie is also facing terrorism, child abuse and torture charges in two other courts.
Francis Wanje, a 62-year-old teacher who lost two grandchildren, told AFP he had hoped Mackenzie would be sentenced to death to prevent further tragedies.

"Nothing can ease the pain," said Wanje, who blamed authorities for failing to act swiftly. "I really have great (anger) towards the authorities. If they had taken action, we would not be here today."
Case exposed
Mackenzie was arrested in April 2023, after a rights group tipped off authorities and some followers were rescued.
The subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of shallow graves, with a soaring death toll that required a pause in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.
The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights said in 2024 that the death toll was 429. Some victims are still unidentified.
Mackenzie has a history of extremism and evaded law enforcement for years.
He established the Good News International Church in 2003, and set up branches in Nairobi and along Kenya's coast that attracted thousands of devotees, though he claimed it closed in 2019.

Followers have told their families and officials they believed Mackenzie when he preached that starvation was the path to salvation. He allegedly split members into smaller groups assigned biblical names. It's believed these smaller groups died together and were buried together in mass graves.
State pathologists have said many of the exhumed victims died of starvation, but some showed signs of strangulation.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2017 over charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.

Investigators have said Mackenzie was a taxi driver in the early 2000s, before he created the Good News International Ministry. Locals have said he quickly drew followers with fiery sermons at his church on the coast in Malindi, then from across Kenya with his online presence.

Several surviving members of the group have told family members that what he preached would often come true, citing as an example his prediction that "a great virus" would come, just before COVID-19 hit the country. As people struggled during the pandemic, financially and medically, Mackenzie preached about leaving the difficulties of life behind and "turning to salvation."

title: 3 charged with using AI to steal some $129 million from companies
summary: Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted, prosecutors say.
story: New York — Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday.

Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York.

Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents.
The defendants, from Spain, the U.K., Israel and the United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment.

Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit didn't immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It wasn't clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York didn't immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press.
The three were arrested between June and September — Soall and Hazan in Spain and Sheetrit in the U.K. Extradition requests for all three are pending.
In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

The trio, who have nicknames that include "Rocky Balboa," "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy," often targeted the companies' accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents.
They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment.
The defendants would then tell them to contact an attorney at a major law firm, who the group was also ready to impersonate, according to court documents.

Soall mainly impersonated attorneys from the U.K. and had a "handwritten script titled 'Lawyer Call' that he utilized to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with and defrauding victims," according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

The impersonated attorney would tell the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts across the world, according to court documents. The funds were then converted into cryptocurrency to try to conceal where they came from and then distributed to the trio and others involved, according to court documents.
FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. said the case shows how advanced technology can be used to commit large-scale fraud.

"As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities," he said in a statement.
If convicted, the defendants face a maximum sentence of 20 years, except for aggravated identity theft, which has a maximum sentence of two years, according to the attorney's office.

title: Grim details emerge after bear kills woman and daughter
summary: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bear's behavior.
story: Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.

When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.

Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.

The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.

Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year's attack.

"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
Bear attack complicated the search
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.

Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache — a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.

By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Balcarras was comfortable in challenging environments

Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.

Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.

"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.

"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."
Other bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

title: French workers flood streets for anti-government protests
summary: Thousands of government workers, teachers, transport employees and other union workers in France walked off the job Thursday to express their frustration with low wages and the high cost of living.
story: Tens of thousands of government workers, teachers, transport employees and other union workers in France walked off the job Thursday to take part in the latest round of massive economic protests that have roiled the European nation, expressing their frustration with low wages and the high cost of living.
What was billed as a national day of action started with nearly 200 peaceful rallies across the country.

The General Confederation of Labour, or GCL, one of France's major unions, said that about 1.6 million people took to the streets, while France's Interior Ministry pegged the number much lower, at about 600,000.
The demonstrations even briefly shut down the Eiffel Tower.
"Our salaries do not allow us to live anymore," Sophie Binet, the head of GCL, told CBS News when asked why the ongoing demonstrations have taken center stage in France.
Binet urged supporters to continue the protests and accused French President Emmanuel Macron of not hearing the people's cries for help.
"Because he thinks he knows everything alone," Binet said of Macron. "Because he works for the rich, for the … multinational and for the finance, not for the working people."
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu  on Monday called for a meeting with the unions, but another protest is already scheduled for this coming Saturday.

Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis, a Paris suburb, told CBS News that Macron is "incapable of bringing answers," saying that protesters are "fed up with having a society that is more and more privileged — the strongest in the world that leaves behind an ocean of inequalities."
Several protesters told CBS News they want to see the French government reduce its military and domestic law enforcement spending and boost funding of social services.
Thursday's rallies turned violent in some areas, ending with the use of tear gas by police to clear out protesters. Clashes broke out during several of the demonstrations.
Protesters torched a car in the central French city of Lyon and burned objects on the streets of Paris.

The anti-government demonstrations first began in late September among high school and university students in Paris who were protesting poor school conditions, teacher shortages and infrastructure issues. They quickly spread and gained a wider backing, with local surveys showing nearly six in 10 people in France support them.

In many instances, though, the protests have degenerated into violence, with buildings and landmarks burned, small businesses vandalized, and clashes with police that led to thousands of arrests. At the height of the violence last month, curfews were issued in several cities.

title: Spacewalkers complete space station solar power upgrade
summary: The eighth and final roll-out solar array installation caps a five-year effort to augment the space station's aging, original solar wings.
story: Completing a complex upgrade five years in the making, two spacewalking astronauts on Thursday mounted an eighth and final roll-out solar wing on the International Space Station, boosting the lab's power output to compensate for the age-related degradation of its original arrays.

NASA began the power-system upgrade in 2021 when two spacewalkers installed the first ISS roll-out solar array, or IROSA, at the base of one of the original eight wings. Six additional panels were attached during subsequent spacewalks, with the most recent installation carried out last week during a spacewalk by NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk.

The duo ventured back outside Thursday to install the eighth and final IROSA on the far right end of the station's power truss, beginning the extravehicular activity, or EVA — NASA speak for "spacewalk" — at 8:36 a.m. ET.

The final two IROSAs were delivered to the station aboard a SpaceX Cargo Dragon capsule earlier this month, with each one folded in half and stowed in the ship's unpressurized trunk section. The lab's robot arm mounted both rolled-up blankets on the left side of the station's power truss to await installation.

Attachment and extension of the seventh panel last week was relatively straightforward because the 58-foot-long robot arm could easily carry Menon, holding onto a new IROSA, to its nearby installation point on a fixture at the base of an inboard left-side solar wing.

But the Canadarm II does not have the reach to carry Menon and the final blanket directly to the far right end of the power truss as required, so he and Kutryk handed it off to each other leapfrog fashion to get it all the way out to a waiting support frame.

Once mounted on the base of the outboard array, Menon and Kutryk unfolded the new IROSA, bolted it in place, and connected power and data cables during orbital darkness when no sunlight was available to generate electricity.

As the station moved back into sunlight, flight controllers noticed one of the two still-rolled-up blankets did not appear to be generating a small amount of electricity as expected. The spacewalkers then waited for another night pass to double-check the connections. The problem was resolved, and the final IROSA blankets were extended to their full length of 63 feet.

"These solar arrays are incredible, half the size of the old ones. It's delivering 40% more power," Menon said after returning to the airlock. "It's really empowering all this research that we do and everything that we do to transform space and open the doors to the future."
The six-hour, 59-minute spacewalk ended at 3:35 p.m.
The IROSAs were designed to offset age-related degradation that has reduced the power output of the station's original arrays over more than two decades of use in the harsh space environment.
The new panels are smaller but more efficient, featuring state-of-the-art solar cells. Even though they shade portions of the arrays they are mounted on, they still provide a net boost in power.

Before the first IROSA was installed, the original arrays were generating about 160 kilowatts of power. The eighth and final IROSA was expected to boost the total power output to some 215 kilowatts, enough to sustain the lab through its planned retirement and de-orbiting in 2030, powering life support systems, computers, research and visiting vehicles.

title: Mexican judge accused by U.S. of taking bribes in major drug case
summary: Luiz Benítez Alcántara is accused of releasing Andrew Clark from custody after accepting $2 million in bribe payments.
story: A Mexican judge has been arrested and accused of accepting $2 million in bribes in exchange for releasing a suspected Canadian drug trafficker from custody, U.S. officials said Thursday.

Luiz Benítez Alcántara was overseeing extradition proceedings in Mexico in 2024 for Canadian citizen Andrew Clark, who was charged in the U.S. with helping to run a billion-dollar drug trafficking group allegedly headed by former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, the Justice Department said in a statement. Benítez is accused of releasing Clark from custody after accepting the bribe payments, according to the statement.
Clark was arrested days after his release and removed to the United States, where he faces drug trafficking and murder charges.
The statement said Benítez, 49, was arrested Sunday in Colombia. He is charged in a nine-count indictment with being an accessory after the fact. It was not immediately known if he has a lawyer.
U.S. officials will request Benítez's extradition from Colombia, the statement said.

"Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement.

It's the latest arrest in the U.S. investigation into a multinational drug trafficking network allegedly run by Wedding, who became a top FBI fugitive accused of moving cocaine from Latin America into the United States and orchestrating several killings. Wedding was arrested in Mexico earlier this year and flown to California, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and drug charges.

Dozens of people have been arrested in connection with the alleged drug network and authorities seized large volumes of drugs, weapons and cash, as well as millions of dollars worth of automobiles, motorcycles, artwork and jewelry in its investigation.
Clark's attorney, Matthew Lombard, did not immediately respond to messages Thursday.

After Wedding's arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel called the former Olympian "a modern-day 'El Chapo,'" — a reference to Joaquin Guzman, a one-time leader of the notorious Mexican drug ring known as the Sinaloa Cartel who is serving a life sentence in the U.S. According to the FBI, Wedding also used aliases, including "El Jefe," "Giant" and "Public Enemy."

Wedding, who competed in the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City, has been accused of running a major drug trafficking network that moved cocaine from Colombia through Mexico to the U.S. and Canada. Patel said in a social media post Friday that Wedding was running his alleged operation as a member of the Sinaloa Cartel, and that Wedding was believed to have been hiding out in Mexico for over a decade.
Wedding was added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list last year, prior to his arrest.

title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
summary: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
story: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three other women on Thursday at his trial in London. Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand will be sentenced to prison.

Brand, 51, was initially accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault. On Thursday, he was acquitted of two rape counts and the attempted indecent assault charge.

"You've been convicted of a number of offences including rape," Bennathan told Brand after reading Thursday's verdict, according to CBS News partner BBC. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody."
Brand, who was denied bail and taken into custody, will be sentenced on Monday.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said, according to the Associated Press. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
The allegations, made by six women, spanned a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days. They found Brand guilty of grabbing a woman's breasts during a party at a bar in London's Soho neighborhood in the summer of 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at London radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005, and raping a woman at his home in Hampstead in 2009.

Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.
During the trial, a prosecutor accused Brand of being a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator."

Brand, who pleaded not guilty to the charges, testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man. He said he once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will, saying he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
He said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
During the trial, Brand suggested the reports were part of a coordinated attack because of his newfound prominence as an online wellness influencer and political commentator.

The women featured in the documentary said they only felt ready to share their stories after being approached by reporters, with some mentioning Brand's online fame as a factor in their decision to speak.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."
Brand's father, Ron Brand, told the BBC after the verdict and that he was "bemused and shocked."
"I just didn't expect this - it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating."

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek" and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

title: Ronaldo retires from Portugal national team
summary: Cristiano Ronaldo says he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.
story: Lisbon, Portugal — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.

The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. "I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

"Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end."

While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.

Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn't plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team's training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.
The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing "deep gratitude and immense admiration" for Ronaldo's service to the country.

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" the federation said.
It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."
Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.
He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and has 985. Of those, a record 146 came in 234 appearances with Portugal.
Ronaldo became the first player in his sport to reach billionaire status, joining the ranks of the wealthiest athletes, Bloomberg reported in October 2025..

Michael Sanft, the Las Vegas defense attorney who represented Duane "Keffe D" Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder case, was found dead inside his home Friday morning, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal. He was 55.
The cause and manner of Sanft's death has not yet been determined. Police told the Las Vegas outlet that the death did not appear suspicious.
Michael Sloan, a close friend who rode motorcycles with Sanft, according to the report, confirmed his death and remembered the attorney as a devoted friend.

story: (Video courtesy: The Sun) Meghan Markle's estranged father, 82, was arrested in Florida and charged with possession of child sexual abuse images following an FBI investigation.
Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle Sr., has spent years in the public eye following his highly publicized falling-out with the Duchess of Sussex ahead of her 2018 royal wedding.

Meghan's relationship with her father deteriorated publicly in May 2018, as she was set to marry Prince Harry. Just days before the royal wedding, he became embroiled in a controversy involving staged paparazzi photographs.

title: Bill Paxton's son takes on Western role late father never got to play: 'I could literally hear my dad'
summary: James Paxton steps into the Western role his late father Bill Paxton was cast in over 30 years ago, calling the film a "conduit" to connect with him.
story: "Last Train to Fortune" star James Paxton tells Fox News Digital how playing a Western role originally intended for his late father became a deeply personal way to reconnect with the "Twister" star.
Bill Paxton's son, James Paxton, is carrying on his late father's legacy by taking on a Western role that the "Twister" star was originally set to play more than 30 years ago.

In 1991, Bill was cast alongside Malcolm McDowell in the Western comedy drama "Last Train to Fortune," but the project stalled following original director Lindsay Anderson’s death in 1994. "Last Train to Fortune" spent decades trapped in development but efforts to revive the movie were gaining momentum again in 2017 when Bill unexpectedly died, leaving the role that would ultimately be played by James.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, James, 32, opened up about how the project became a deeply personal way to reconnect with Bill, who passed away in February 2017 following heart surgery.
'DEADPOOL' STAR ROB DELANEY REVEALS HOW LOSING 2-YEAR-OLD SON CHANGED HIS APPROACH TO FAME
Bill Paton's son, James Paxton, opened up about taking on a Western role that his father was set to play more than 30 years ago. (TriCoast Media; Gregg DeGuire/WireImage)
"When you lose somebody, such a close loved one, you often look for ways to still connect to them," James said.

"And that can take all manner of forms and paths and shapes," he continued. "For me, I recognized immediately that this was the kind of project that I could literally hear my dad in my head the whole time. You know, if I needed any guidance or any motivation, or I had any questions, I knew that he would kind of — he would be right there with me, and he'd be cheering me on for it."
SYLVESTER STALLONE SCOFFS AT NEPOTISM CRITICS OVER DAUGHTER'S 'TULSA KING' ROLE: 'YOU IDIOT'
"So I saw it as a way to — almost like a conduit to commune with him, wherever he is and may be," James added. "And there's something beautiful about following in those footsteps."
James recalled that Bill had his own way of putting his son’s decision to follow him into acting in perspective.
WATCH: BILL PAXTON'S SON SAYS HE COULD 'LITERALLY HEAR' LATE DAD WHILE TAKING ON HIS WESTERN ROLE

"Dad had this metaphor about if this was 100 years ago, and we were a family of shoemakers or cobblers, my father before me was a shoemaker and his father before him, you'd probably go into the family business and become, hopefully, a good shoemaker," James said. "So I've always held that close."

Before Bill's death, he had been working with McDowell and producer Brad Wyman on the "Last Train to Fortune's" revival with Adam Rifkin as director, but financing repeatedly prevented the project from moving forward. After Bill's death, Rifkin, Wyman and McDowell eventually approached James, who previously said that he hadn't even known about the film while his father was alive.
According to Rifkin, the movie was finally able to secure financing once James signed on.
Bringing the project to fruition also had personal significance for Adam, whose late mother, Michele Rifkin, penned the original script for a PBS screenwriting competition in 1986.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
James said he could "literally hear" Bill's voice while filming.  (TriCoast Worldwide)
"It was always her son Adam's dream to bring the film to life," James said.

James recalled that Michele had been unable to visit the set as she was bedridden in the hospital during the movie's production. However, the late screenwriter had the opportunity to see James and McDowell in costume when the duo FaceTimed her during filming.

"She told us that when she saw us in costume it was like we had walked right out of her imagination up off the page and into the real world," he remembered. "And that was so touching, and it immediately made me think about my dad in that moment."

"Michele passed away not long after that, and she got to see the finished film before it was released privately, which was amazing, but it made me think all the more about my dad," James said. "Because I know that he … would've wanted us to make this even if he was still around, if they had never got off the ground. He would have been like, ‘James, here, this is your role,’ and so that kind of really made me think of him in that moment in particular."
SCOTT EASTWOOD CREDITS HIS FAMOUS FATHER'S WORK ETHIC FOR MAKING HIM AWARE OF 'BULLS---' IN THE FILM INDUSTRY
Malcolm McDowell, who was originally set to star opposite Bill, co-starred alongside James. (TriCoast Worldwide)
Although James was stepping into a role once intended for his father, he said he knew Bill would have wanted him to find his own approach to the character.

"It was totally important for me to create my own version just because I know what Dad would tell me," he said. "And it's tough for me because he was my best friend, so all I wanna do is talk about him and celebrate him, but he goes, 'You're your own actor. You've been studying this. You're a professional.'"
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I've done a lot of work actually in the past years that he's been gone," James continued. "But I know that he always wanted me to make it my own, and he would be like, 'Don't hitch up on my wagon too much, you'll find it in yourself.' But he would just give me these great acting pieces of advice and wisdom. So I knew that he wouldn't want me to focus on that. He'd say, 'Focus on, it's the character's moment to live, it's Jedediah Dooley's moment to come to life.' So it's not James up there, it's not Bill up there, it's the character."

While Bill encouraged his son to forge his own path as an actor, James recalled that his father was equally determined for his children to develop discipline in other areas of their lives. Along with James, Bill shared daughter Lydia with his wife, Louise Newbury.
James recalled how his late father had a "drill sergeant" side. (Getty Images)

"He didn't love it when my sister and I would sleep in too late," James remembered. "He was a bit of a drill sergeant when it came to just getting up and doing something. So he would come in, and I became almost like — it was Pavlovian. As a kid, I became conditioned to hear his footsteps coming down the hall. And if I wasn't sitting up and out of my bed by the time he came in the room, he'd rip the sheets off of me, and he'd go, 'Rise and shine, you're burning daylight out here.'"

"And he just put up the blinds, and it would just flood the room with blinding light and I would freak out a bit," James continued. "But he'd get me going, and so I — even in my half-asleep state — I could jolt awake when I'd hear him coming. Even on the weekends, if he was home, he'd be like, ‘Come on man, get up and do something.’ He wasn't controlling about what that was, but it was about motivating me not to just stay in bed."
James recalled how Bill also wanted his son to have real-life experiences and not define himself solely through acting.
WATCH: BILL PAXTON'S SON RECALLS 'DRILL SERGEANT' DAD RIPPING SHEETS OFF HIM FOR SLEEPING IN

"I used to have a ton of all kinds of odd jobs," James recalled. "I worked in tons of restaurants. I apprenticed as a tile maker. I worked for UPS. I had a lot of really cool experiences. I scooped ice cream, that was my first job. And those were largely thanks to dad encouraging me to do that."
Though James said Bill supported his acting ambitions, he recalled that his father tried to prepare him for the realities of working in Hollywood.

"I would say he was probably more concerned with warning me about all of the pitfalls and the hardships that can fall," James said. "Even somebody as successful as he was in his career, he ran the gamut of every Hollywood experience and every disappointment.

"And he always talked about it's the time between jobs where you really can suffer," he continued. "'The death of a thousand paper cuts.' he would call it. You have to find something that can buoy you between jobs, and you don't put your self-worth in it."
James said that Bill warned him about the "pitfalls" of Hollywood. (WireImage)

"If anything, he was like, ‘Man if you want to do anything else like, even just as much as this, do that instead,’" James recalled. "He was like, ‘This is a hard thing’ and so if anything, he kind of gave me this extra chip on my shoulder because I was like, 'Well, I'm gonna go, and I'm going to book something and show him.'"

James made his career breakthrough in the USA Network crime thriller drama "Eyewitness," which premiered in October 2016. While speaking with Fox News Digital, James recalled Bill's reaction when he landed the leading role of Lukas Waldenbeck in the series.

"He almost couldn't believe it, but there was this huge sense of relief," James said. "And he called it a ‘real ticket to ride,' as in, it was his way of saying, 'This is a real opportunity. Now you go and show them and stuff. You've done the work to get here.'"
"So that was really cool," he continued. "He saw that right before he passed, which was amazing."

Since starring in "Eyewitness," James has steadily built his acting career with appearances in projects including "Training Day," "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.," "Tacoma FD" and "The Cleaner." In 2024, he made a cameo in "Twisters," the standalone sequel to his father’s 1996 blockbuster "Twister."

"I still get the whole 'it's Bill Paxton's son' thing, but I have over 45 acting credits," James told Fox News Digital. "But I laugh it off. As Dad would say, man it's all just — it's a great experience, and you're on the path."
James said Bill felt a "huge sense of relief" when he landed his breakthrough role in "Eyewitness." (AFP via Getty Images)

In "Last Train to Fortune," McDowell's character Cecil Peachtree misses the last train to his new teaching job in the frontier town of Fortune and enlists the help of James' Jedidiah Booley to get him there safely, with the mismatched pair forming an unlikely bond along the way.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

In addition to their long-held plans to co-star in the movie, McDowell and Bill were close friends and neighbors in Ojai, California. James told Fox News Digital that McDowell recently reminded him of a story that illustrated how the "Clockwork Orange" star's friendship with his father extended far beyond Hollywood.
"Last Train to Fortune" arrives on VOD Nov. 6th  (TriCoast Worldwide)

"I grew up in the Ojai Valley, and we've obviously been plagued by a lot of wildfires over the years," he said. "And it was a pretty bad one when I was quite young. I can't recall exactly, it was early 2000s. Malcolm had a property that was kind of up in the hills, backing up against a lot of wildlife, ground, and forest. And the fire was coming up on his property, and he said that he saw Dad show up in full volunteer fireman regalia, like the full suit, ready to fight the fire with Malcolm.

"And there's a great photo that Kelly, Malcolm's wife, sent to me of the two of them," he continued. "We'll have to track it down because it's great. It's them, you know, they took a quick picture as they were fighting the fire and protecting the Ojai Valley. So I loved the thought of them working together on something outside of film, in real life."
WATCH: BILL PAXTON WARNED SON ABOUT HOLLYWOOD'S 'DEATH OF A THOUSAND PAPER CUTS'
When asked what he believed would make his father most proud of the person he has become, James pointed to his determination to keep going despite the difficult moments he has faced.

"I think he'd be most proud that I have never given up," James said. "I think the perseverance. I think that if our past loved ones can see us at times, they can see our energy or something, they can see us from another place while we're alive, they'd see that there's often like moments of true despair."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I mean, I would be lying if I said I didn't come close to giving up on a lot of things many times and being like, 'What's the point to keep it going?', but then I realize that's just a wallowing pity party," he continued. "You've got to recognize the blessings and the privilege and keep it going. He's like, ‘I set this up for you.' And so I just want him to know that I'm always gonna honor what he gave me.""Last Train to Fortune" arrives on VOD Nov. 6th

title: 'Jimmy' star Jen Lilley says keeping Jesus at center of marriage helped through 'extremely difficult times'
summary: Hallmark star Jen Lilley tells Fox News Digital how portraying Gloria Stewart in the biopic "Jimmy" reinforced her own marriage values rooted in faith.
story: "Jimmy" star and Hallmark actress Jen Lilley tells Fox News Digital she’s turned down Hollywood roles to put her husband and four children first.
Hollywood has seen its fair share of high-profile breakups, but Jen Lilley says the secret to her nearly 20-year marriage has nothing to do with fame, fortune or romance.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, the "Jimmy" star credited putting Jesus first with helping her and her husband get through some of life's most challenging moments.
For Lilley, the secret isn't a Hollywood-approved relationship trick or a carefully guarded marriage formula.
WILLIE ROBERTSON'S FAITH-BASED ADVICE THAT'S KEPT HIS 34-YEAR MARRIAGE TO WIFE KORIE STRONG
Actress Jen Lilley says she's turned down Hollywood roles to protect her family, putting her children and marriage ahead of career opportunities. (Jen Lilley / Morgan Raum )
"This is just something that I can say for me personally. You know, maybe it's not the secret for other people, but we both, we have a really strong faith," Lilley told Fox News Digital.
"And I think that for us, keeping Jesus at the center of our marriage has really been what has gotten us through extremely difficult times," she said.
WATCH: JEN LILLEY WON'T LET HOLLYWOOD GET IN THE WAY OF HER FAMILY
Lilley said her commitment to faith also influences the roles she takes in Hollywood.
CHRIS PRATT SAYS HIS FAITH WILL BE 'THE MOST IMPORTANT THING' THAT HE PASSES ON TO HIS KIDS
While many actors chase the next big opportunity, Lilley says no role is worth sacrificing for her brood.

"I think the values that I hold onto are actually common to most people, but I really value my family. I will make decisions based on the well-being of my own children and my marriage, even when sometimes it's not what I want," she said.
"There have been times I've had to turn down a role or something because it just doesn't fit what I need in this season."
Hallmark star Jen Lilley credits keeping Jesus at the center of her nearly 20-year marriage with helping her and her husband overcome difficult times. (Jen Lilley)
"The values that I've carried are just really making sure that you're loving your family and your neighbor well," she added.
Lilley married engineer Jason Wayne in 2007, and the couple share four children, including two sons adopted through foster care and two daughters.
In her latest project, the actress portrays Gloria Stewart, the wife of Hollywood legend Jimmy Stewart, in the biopic "Jimmy."
While preparing for the part, Lilley discovered a love story that went far beyond the glamour of Hollywood.
TIM ALLEN REVEALS THE ONE THING THAT HAS SAVED HIS NEARLY 20-YEAR MARRIAGE TO JANE HAJDUK
Actor Jimmy Stewart and his wife Gloria step out of a car to attend the premiere of the film "The Country Girl" on Jan. 27, 1955. (Bettmann / Getty Images)
"I think what surprised me the most was just how much they enjoyed each other's company their entire lives," she told Fox News Digital.

Jimmy Stewart, once dubbed Hollywood's eternal bachelor, found lasting love with Gloria, who brought two sons from a previous marriage into their relationship. Stewart adopted the boys, and the couple later welcomed two daughters together.
But their marriage faced challenges that went far beyond Hollywood.

Lilley said Stewart returned from serving in World War II with symptoms she described as consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), at a time when the condition was not yet formally recognized under that name.
She described Gloria as the actor's emotional anchor — someone who could navigate Hollywood's elite social circles but also provide a safe haven when the cameras stopped rolling.
WATCH: JIMMY STEWART'S FINAL WISH STRIKES A CHORD WITH ACTRESS JEN LILLEY
Lilley told Fox News Digital portraying Gloria also gave her a fresh perspective on what keeps a marriage standing when life gets messy — trust, laughter and having someone who feels like home.
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY
"I think what made their marriage really work was the fact that they did have so much trust with each other, and they had a lot of humor," she said.
Actor James Stewart, his wife, Gloria, and children on July 1, 1960. (Tom Baffer / New York Daily News via Getty Images)
"I mean, I think that if you don't have a sense of humor, good luck getting through life. You know, life has a perfectly adequate way of knocking you back down often."

The lesson hit close to home for Lilley, who said the Stewarts' relationship reinforced the importance of finding laughter even during difficult seasons and being a dependable source of comfort for a spouse.

"And so, I think for my own marriage it just encouraged me that, you know, you can always find something to laugh at even when times are hard and just to be consistent and safe with each other," she said.
Jen Lilley as Gloria Stewart in "Jimmy."  (Burns & Co., © 2026 JIMMY The Movie LLC)
The Hallmark actress called playing Gloria Stewart a dream come true.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
WATCH HERE: NEW MOVIE PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON JIMMY STEWART'S LIFE, ACTOR CHRISTOPHER MCDONALD SAYS

"I have always been a huge fan of Jimmy Stewart, his movies and his life philosophy," she previously said. "It is a dream come true to step into the role of the love of his life. This film is beautiful and will be beloved by many."
The film is also offering free tickets to veterans, a gesture Lilley praised as an opportunity to honor those who served.
"Jimmy," a film based on the story of actor Jimmy Stewart hits theaters November 6, 2026. (Burns & Co., © 2026 JIMMY The Movie LLC)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Away from Hollywood, the actress has also advocated for foster children, drawing on her experiences as a foster and adoptive parent. She co-authored "Called to Foster" to encourage more families to open their homes to children in need.

She also relaunched her "Christmas Is Not Canceled" campaign, which began in 2020 and helped deliver gifts to 10,000 children. The 2026 initiative encourages toy donations for children in need, with donors entered to win a Hallmark-style Christmas prize package.

title: Meghan Markle's father arrested in Florida
summary: Authorities arrested Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle's dad, in Florida on Friday, according to a law enforcement source.
story: U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli and The Sun editor-at-large Harry Cole discuss the arrest of Thomas Markle on a federal charge of child sexual abuse material on ‘America Reports.’
Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle, has been arrested in Florida.

Markle Sr. appeared in court Friday for his initial appearance, accompanied by several U.S. marshals. After ordering Markle to undergo a psychological evaluation to determine whether he understands the charges against him, the judge released him without requiring bond.

He is subject to having his location monitored at all times and ordered not to travel outside the United States. His defense attorney claimed Markle Sr. did not know where his passport was at this time.
Markle will be held under home detention at the memory care facility where he was arrested.
READ THE COMPLAINT:

Meghan's dad, who is wheelchair-bound after losing a leg, wore black pants and a black T-shirt featuring a cat wearing sunglasses and holding an iced coffee. Markle scowled and glared at people in the front row of the courtroom. He was provided with a public defender and asked if he understood the charges.
Markle was given the option to have his case proceed in California rather than Florida. If he chooses California, he will have to remain in custody and be transported.
MEGHAN MARKLE SAYS SHE KEPT FATHER AWAY FROM KIDS TO ‘PROTECT’ THEM OVER ‘DISTURBING ALLEGATIONS’ AGAINST HIM
Retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack told Fox News Digital what will happen next as the investigation continues.

"Investigators will keep examining the seized material, working to identify and protect any children who may have been harmed, and checking whether the evidence points to other victims or offenses," Pack explained. The affidavit says that review is still underway.
Markle's dementia diagnosis matters but "doesn’t automatically end the case," Pack emphasized.
Meghan Markle said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations against her father. (Getty Images)

"The court may need to determine whether he understands the proceedings and can help his lawyer," he added. "That is different from asking whether a mental illness affected his responsibility at the time of the alleged conduct. Those are legal questions for the judge, supported by medical evidence."

"There’s going to be a court of public opinion because this is a high-profile family and the allegations are disturbing. But headlines and family history don’t decide guilt," Pack said. "The focus needs to stay on protecting any children who may have been harmed and letting the evidence be tested in court. A federal charge is serious. The government still has to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt."

Federal prosecutors charged Markle Sr. with possession of child pornography in a criminal complaint filed Nov. 5.

According to the 14-page complaint obtained by Fox News Digital, FBI agents searched two storage units registered to Markle and seized approximately 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material. Investigators say Markle had rented the units since 2008 and continued paying for them through October 2026.

Agents identified approximately 18 suspected illegal images among film negatives recovered from one unit.

Despite having surgery just a week earlier, Barroso got dressed up and accompanied her husband to an Oscars after-party, determined not to let another major Hollywood moment pass them by.

title: Russell Brand found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault
summary: Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in a U.K. court on Thursday. He is expected to be sentenced on Monday.
story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett reports as Russell Brand faces trial in London over allegations of rape and sexual assault on 'America Reports.'

Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in the U.K. He denied the charges and was acquitted of two additional rape charges and attempted indecent assault.
He has been taken into custody and is due to be sentenced Monday, according to BBC.
Brand, 51, was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009.
RUSSELL BRAND ACCUSED OF RAPE, SEXUAL ABUSE OF 4 WOMEN; COMEDIAN DENIES ‘SERIOUS CRIMINAL ALLEGATIONS’

According to Sky News, Brand acknowledged that he had been "reckless" and used his fame to pursue sexual relationships, but insisted that the encounters were consensual. He also told the jury that consent was "fundamental, essential and necessary."
Brand has denied forcing any of the women to engage in sexual activity against their will.
Last week, Brand's wife, Laura Brand, took the stand as a defense witness, one day after the comedian and actor testified.
During Laura's testimony, the mom of three — who first met her husband when she was 19, and he was 31 — opened up about the start of their relationship.

"I was not interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people. title: Paris Jackson demands $600M from father Michael Jackson's estate in legal war with longtime executor
summary: Paris Jackson accused executor John Branca of financial retaliation after she challenged his handling of Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate.
story: Victoria Price told Fox News Digital that as long as there is Halloween, people will listen to the horror icon's narration in the hit song.

Paris Jackson accused John Branca, the sole executor of her late father Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate, of financially retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the King of Pop's fortune.

Paris alleged in new court documents obtained by Fox News Digital, that she and her siblings experienced a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments while Branca maintained an "iron grip" over their inheritance.
She asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from her late father's estate into the family trust after accusing Branca of mismanaging the funds.
PARIS JACKSON SAYS DAD MICHAEL'S UNUSAL RULE HELPED PROTECT HER CHILDHOOD
Paris Jackson asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from Michael Jackson’s estate to the family trust. (Alan Chapman/Getty Images)
Branca has been the sole executor of Jackson's estate since 2009. The pop star died that year from acute propofol and sedative intoxication leading to cardiac arrest.

Branca's alleged mismanagement of estate funds included non-contractual gifts to colleagues, aggressive litigation, public attacks and a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments to Jackson's children.

"Without belaboring the point, when Paris began challenging the administration of the Estate last year through her objection to Executor Branca’s non-contractual gifts to his colleagues, her challenges were met with scorched earth litigation, public attacks, and a multimillion reduction in monies provided to her and her siblings by the Estate," her legal team wrote. "This course of conduct and administration should not continue."
Paris Jackson is the daughter of Michael Jackson and Debbie Rowe. (Swan Gallet/WWD/Getty Images)

In a separate filing obtained by Fox News Digital, Paris accused Branca of using estate resources for personal travel on private jets, improperly charging personal expenses to the estate and concealing the spending from beneficiaries.

She claimed Branca acknowledged taking multiple personal trips and reimbursed certain expenses only after she investigated them. Her attorneys characterized the conduct as "outright theft" and a breach of his fiduciary duties.
"Where the travel is of a purely personal nature, or in service of Mr. Branca's other clients or business affairs, it constitutes outright theft," the court filing stated.
Prince Jackson and Paris Jackson at the opening night of "MJ: the Musical," at Neil Simon Theatre on Feb. 1, 2022, in New York City. (Bruce Glikas/WireImage)

Paris also accused Branca of using estate funds for personal gifts, questioned more than $604,000 in credit card charges and reimbursements, and challenged $9.4 million in executor compensation, $1.4 million in payments to his law firm and roughly $835,000 in public relations expenses.

She further alleged that Branca mismanaged more than $440 million in estate cash while pursuing entertainment projects that benefited him financially, including the Michael Jackson biopic, which reportedly required tens of millions of dollars in reshoots and rewrites.
Her legal team urged the court to reject Branca's financial accounting and order him to provide a more detailed breakdown of the estate's spending.

"Once again, Ms. Jackson’s legal team raises the same hollow complaints and fails to acknowledge the unique structure of the Estate, which is operated as a dynamic business, with customary costs and expenses," a representative for the estate told Fox News Digital. "No rhetoric can hide the fact that the Executors have taken an Estate that was $500 million in debt when Michael died and turned it into the most successful Estate in history, producing $3 billion in revenue and the biggest biopic in movie history, with a box office exceeding $1 billion globally."

From left to right, Michael Jackson's kids Prince Jackson, Blanket Jackson and Paris Jackson, LaToya Jackson and Katherine Jackson attend Children's Hospital Los Angeles Receives Michael Jackson Artwork Donation ceremony on Aug. 8, 2011, in Los Angeles. (Valerie Macon/Getty Images)

A representative for Paris told Fox News Digital: "No rhetoric can hide the fact that Mr. Branca has used Estate funds to create a lavish lifestyle complete with charging personal trips on private jets to the Estate. This wasteful spending and financial mismanagement flies in the face of his fiduciary duty to the beneficiaries and has gone unchecked for too long."

As for the $600 million distribution, Paris argued that her father's estate plan entitled his children — Prince, Paris and Bigi — to trust income beginning at age 21 and portions of their inheritance beginning at age 30. She claimed the executor had never funded the trust, despite Michael Jackson's death more than 17 years earlier.

Paris Jackson accused Michael Jackson's executor, John Branca, of retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the estate. (Rita Barros/Getty Images)

"Michael intended for his children to become the caretakers of his legacy," the petition read. "As each child reached certain ages, Executors were to increasingly provide for each child’s independence."

Paris' filing cited more than $2.5 billion in gross estate earnings and approximately $850 million in cash or cash equivalents as of December 2024. She argued that the estate could distribute $600 million while retaining enough money to cover outstanding liabilities.

"Ms. Jackson’s counsel is well aware that the Estate is prevented from fully funding the philanthropic giving and individual trusts for the beneficiaries until several legal hurdles have been removed, including in particular the ongoing IRS litigation where they sought $700 million in taxes and penalties from the Estate," a statement provided to Fox News Digital on behalf of Jackson's estate said. "The Estate was able to secure a ruling to significantly reduce that amount, but the matter has not been settled and could still change."

"Further, the claim that the executor has withheld or ‘cut' payments is a complete fabrication," the statement added. "In fact, more than $200 million has already been distributed for the benefit of Paris and the other beneficiaries. Michael Jackson’s will is clear. None of his children receive a distribution until they are in their 30s. The Estate looks forward to the time when all issues are resolved so that their trusts can be fully funded as Michael wanted."

A representative for Paris told Fox News Digital: "The Estate is once again deflecting from its own incompetence. Paris called for the trust to be partially funded, something Mr. Branca had the ability and obligation to do long ago. After years of delay, Paris had no choice but to step in herself."

Paris previously spoke about her childhood as the daughter of Michael Jackson. Behind the glitz of Jackson’s larger-than-life world, Paris said her father enforced strict rules to protect his children’s sense of normalcy.

The 28-year-old model recalled in an interview on "Call Her Daddy" that her father required his children to finish their homework and chores before enjoying weekend activities, limited their television and movie viewing, and had them wear masks in public to shield their identities from the intense spotlight surrounding his fame.
Paris said she understood that her father was famous. What she didn’t grasp was the sheer magnitude of his celebrity.

"I just didn't know how famous ... There was definitely part of me that, like when I looked out my hotel window, and it was one of the times where, like, the alias didn't work and there's just like a sea of people with signs and stuff — I'm not so naive to think, yeah, everyone experiences this, you know?"
